top_learned_concepts: Exception handling in C#, especially try/catch and basic error-handling flow, was the clearest learning theme.
A smaller cluster reported learning file I/O concepts, especially StreamReader, parsing data from files, and saving/input-output with files.
Some students framed the week as learning debugging-oriented practices and writing more user-friendly error behavior.
top_struggle_clusters: Exceptions were both learned and still uncertain: students asked about handling all exceptions, choosing exception types, and whether exception logic should be centralized or kept local.
File/data persistence questions remain open, including file size limits, hiding data from users, and whether configuration files are the right storage approach.
Several responses suggest students want broader application context rather than syntax help alone, such as non-text uses of the classes covered, larger-scale error handling, and more examples.
future_interest_clusters: Students want to extend this week's topics into authentic applications: web UI error messages, save data/save points, and large-scale exception handling.
There is continued interest in transferring ideas across contexts, including other languages and similar classes used for different purposes.
A smaller exploratory cluster points beyond this week to search algorithms, game development, hardware-focused topics, and vector arrays.
mismatches: Exception handling appears in both learned and struggled responses, indicating many students grasped the basic syntax but are unsure about design decisions and edge cases.
Top learned terms emphasize try/catch mechanics, while struggle and future responses emphasize when, why, and how broadly to apply them in real programs.
File handling is not dominant in the learned term list overall, but student comments show persistent curiosity about storage, configuration, and save data applications.
teaching_adjustments: Differentiate between 'basic exception syntax' and 'exception design choices' in the next class: when to catch specific exceptions, when not to catch everything, and what makes an error message useful.
Add 1-2 worked examples that connect exceptions with file I/O and persistence, since students are asking about configs, save data, and file-based applications.
Include a brief discussion of scope and architecture: whether exception handling belongs inline, in helper methods, or in higher-level program layers.
Provide one 'real-world scale' example, such as error handling in a web page or larger application, to answer interest in what this looks like beyond toy programs.
Consider a short FAQ or mini-lecture on data storage decisions: plain text files, config files, and what 'hidden' or protected data means at the user/file-system level.
Use debugging support alongside exception handling examples, since at least some students are connecting the two topics.
followup_exit_ticket_questions: When writing try/catch blocks, what part feels least clear: choosing what to catch, deciding where to catch it, or deciding what message/action should follow?
After this week, how confident do you feel using file I/O for save data or configuration files, and what specific scenario still feels unclear?
Would a worked example from a console app, a game/save system, or a web page be most helpful for seeing exception handling in context?
What is one design question you still have about exceptions that goes beyond syntax?
ai_summary.short_instructor_summary: Students largely perceived that they learned the basics of exception handling, especially try/catch in C#, with a secondary learning theme around file I/O and StreamReader. The main struggles were not basic syntax so much as application and design: how many exceptions to handle, which types matter, where error-handling code should live, and how file storage choices work in practice. Future-interest responses reinforce this pattern, with students wanting larger-scale, more realistic examples involving web pages, save data, and cross-language transfer. Difficulty appears moderate overall, and the clearest instructional opportunity is to move from mechanics to design-oriented examples and authentic use cases.

study_guide.title: CSCI 1260 Study Guide — Week of 2026-04-17
study_guide.overview: This week’s main review topic is exception handling in C#, especially basic try/catch flow and how it connects to debugging, user-friendly errors, and file I/O. Many students felt okay with the basic syntax, but still want clarification on design decisions: what to catch, whether to catch everything, where exception-handling code should go, and how file-based storage works in realistic programs. Before next class, focus on moving from 'I can write a try/catch' to 'I can explain why this catch belongs here and what should happen next.'
key_takeaways_to_review: Exception handling was the clearest core concept from the week: try/catch, handling errors, and keeping programs from crashing unexpectedly.
Basic error handling is connected to user experience: a program can respond with a clearer message instead of failing silently or stopping abruptly.
File I/O also appeared as an important secondary topic, especially StreamReader, parsing data from files, and saving/input/output with files.
Debugging and exception handling are related but not identical: exceptions help manage runtime problems, while debugging helps you investigate why they happen.
The main next step is not just syntax review, but understanding design choices in realistic programs.
common_sticking_points: Knowing the syntax of try/catch but not knowing which exception types matter in practice.
Wondering whether it is a good idea to handle all exceptions or only specific ones.
Uncertainty about where exception-handling code should live: directly in one method, in helper methods, or in a larger program layer.
Wanting more examples that combine exception handling with file reading, save data, or configuration files.
Questions about file/data usage in real programs, including storage choices and what it means for data to be hidden or protected from users.
practice_prompts: In your own words, explain what a try block does and what a catch block does.
Describe one reason a program might choose to catch a specific exception instead of catching everything broadly.
Write a short plan for how a program should respond if reading a file fails: what should the user see, and what should the program do next?
Think of a small app, game, or webpage. Where might error handling happen in that program, and why there?
Compare these goals: prevent crashes, show useful messages, and keep code organized. How might exception-handling choices affect each one?
example_problems: Given a program that reads from a file, identify at least two places where an exception might occur and describe how the program should respond.
Suppose a catch block only displays a generic 'Something went wrong' message. Rewrite the behavior to be more user-friendly and more helpful for debugging.
A student asks whether all exception-handling code should be moved into its own class. List one possible benefit and one possible drawback of doing that.

Imagine a program that loads configuration data from a file at startup. What should happen if the file is missing, unreadable, or contains bad data? Write a response plan, even if you do not write full code.
practical_examples: A console program reads a text file using StreamReader and should avoid crashing if the file cannot be opened.
A program saves and reloads simple data, such as preferences or save progress, and needs to handle missing or invalid file data gracefully.
A web page or app screen displays a user-friendly error message when an operation fails, instead of exposing a raw technical error.
A larger program may not put every catch block in the same place; some handling may happen near the file operation, while other handling may happen at a higher level of the program.
self_check_questions: Can I explain the difference between learning try/catch syntax and making good exception-handling design decisions?
Do I know at least one reason not to catch every exception in the same way?
Can I describe how exception handling and debugging support each other?
Can I give a realistic example of exception handling with file I/O or save data?
If I saw exception-handling code in a larger project, could I ask whether it belongs locally or at a higher level?
before_next_class: Review your notes on try/catch and exception handling in C#.
Revisit any examples involving StreamReader, file input/output, parsing data, or saving data.
Practice explaining exception behavior in plain language, not just code syntax.
Prepare one question about design, such as what to catch, where to catch it, or how to structure error-handling code.
If helpful, sketch a tiny real-world scenario: loading a config file, reading save data, or showing an error message to a user. Be ready to discuss how exceptions should be handled there.
